source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating tensor parallelism. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer:
Runbook entry: investigating tensor parallelism (TP) on a serving or training deployment.

Assumptions (state these before touching anything): single node, homogeneous GPUs, one model replica per TP group, and a serving engine (vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM) that implements Megatron-style intra-layer sharding. If any assumption is false, the thresholds below change and must be re-measured.

Concrete mechanism. TP shards the weight matrices inside each transformer block, not the layer sequence. In the MLP, the first GEMM is column-parallel (each rank owns hidden_ffn/TP output columns) and the second is row-parallel, so exactly one all-reduce of the activation tensor is required per block after the row-parallel GEMM. Attention is sharded head-wise: each rank owns num_attention_heads/TP query heads and num_key_value_heads/TP KV heads, followed by a second all-reduce after the output projection. So a forward pass costs 2 all-reduces per transformer layer, each of size batch x seq x hidden x dtype_bytes. For a 9B-class model with hidden=4096, bf16, decode with batch=32 and seq=1, that is 32*4096*2 = 256 KB per all-reduce, x2 per layer, x num_layers per token. This is a latency-bound, small-message collective - it is dominated by per-collective launch and link latency, not by bus bandwidth.

Boundary condition (the falsifiable part). TP scales usefully only while the added compute width saves more time than the added collectives cost, and only while every rank in the TP group is connected by a link of the same class. The hard boundary: if the TP group spans a PCIe/QPI hop (nvidia-smi topo -m shows PHB or SYS rather than NV#), small-message all-reduce latency rises by roughly an order of magnitude and decode throughput typically degrades rather than improves. The second hard boundary is divisibility: TP must divide both num_attention_heads and num_key_value_heads. On a GQA model with num_key_value_heads=8, TP=16 cannot shard KV further, so KV heads are replicated, KV-cache memory per GPU stops falling, and the main memory argument for raising TP disappears.

Investigation steps.
1. Record topology: nvidia-smi topo -m, restricted to the exact device set in the TP group. Classify every pair.
2. Establish the collective floor: nccl-tests all_reduce_perf swept over 64 KB - 4 MB (the sizes that actually occur), not only at 1 GB. Record bus bandwidth and latency separately.
3. Read model config for num_attention_heads and num_key_value_heads; enumerate the legal TP degrees.
4. Capture engine startup logs per configuration: usable KV blocks, captured CUDA-graph batch shapes, chunked-prefill state, preemption counters.
5. Benchmark at matched offered load, warmup discarded, reporting TTFT and inter-token latency distributions separately. Never compare a blended tokens/s number across TP degrees - prefill and decode scale differently and a blended figure hides the regression.
6. Confirm the transport actually chosen with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,GRAPH,NET. If the log shows NET/Socket where NVLink was expected, the measurement is about a misconfiguration, not about TP.

Falsifiable prediction. If NVLink is present across the whole group and heads divide evenly, doubling TP should cut per-token decode latency by less than 2x (typically 1.3-1.6x on an 8-GPU NVLink node) and should raise, not lower, achievable batch size via freed KV memory. If measured decode latency rises when TP is doubled, the cause is the collective path or a divisibility violation, not model size.

Rollback gate. Promote a new TP degree only if, on the production traffic mix, p95 TTFT and p95 inter-token latency are both no worse than the incumbent, and no preemption/recompute counter increases. Any single failed criterion means revert to the previous TP degree in the same maintenance window. Keep the old engine process warm until the new one has served the full traffic mix for at least one peak period.

source_user: Define pipeline parallelism and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Definition. Pipeline parallelism (PP) partitions a model by depth: contiguous groups of transformer layers are assigned to different devices (stages), and activations flow stage to stage as point-to-point sends/receives. It is distinct from tensor parallelism, which splits work inside a layer and requires all-reduce collectives; PP moves one activation tensor per stage boundary and needs no collective at all.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure. PP is the parallelism that makes a model fit at all when weights plus optimizer state exceed one device's memory and the interconnect is too weak for wide TP. Because the only cross-device traffic is a single activation tensor of size microbatch x seq x hidden x dtype_bytes per boundary, PP tolerates slow links (PCIe, Ethernet, cross-node) where TP would collapse. This is exactly why real multi-node deployments use TP inside a node (over NVLink) and PP across nodes (over IB/RoCE).

Concrete mechanism: microbatching against the pipeline bubble. With P stages and a single batch, P-1 stages idle at any moment. Splitting the global batch into m microbatches and using a 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) schedule overlaps them, giving bubble fraction approximately (P-1)/(m+P-1). With P=4 and m=1 the bubble is 75%; with m=16 it falls to about 16%; with m=64 to about 4.5%. 1F1B is preferred over naive GPipe scheduling because it caps in-flight activation memory at roughly P microbatches rather than m, at the same bubble fraction. Interleaved (virtual-stage) schedules cut the bubble further by giving each device several non-contiguous layer chunks, at the cost of more stage-boundary transfers.

Boundary condition. The bubble formula only holds while stages are balanced and microbatches are large enough to keep each GPU compute-bound. Two failure regions: (a) if per-stage compute times differ, throughput is set by the slowest stage and adding microbatches does not help - embedding and LM-head stages are the usual offenders and often need explicit layer rebalancing; (b) shrinking the microbatch to raise m eventually pushes each GEMM below the size where the GPU saturates, so per-microbatch time stops falling linearly and total step time rises even though the computed bubble fraction improves. There is therefore an optimum m, and it must be measured, not assumed. A third boundary applies specifically to inference: for autoregressive decode, one token depends on the previous one, so there are few independent microbatches to overlap and PP mostly adds latency; PP helps inference throughput mainly for prefill-heavy or high-concurrency serving, not for single-stream latency.

Evidence to collect before claiming PP is working: per-stage forward/backward wall time (to prove balance), measured bubble from a timeline trace rather than the formula, activation memory high-water mark per stage, stage-boundary transfer size and observed link bandwidth, and step time vs m swept over at least four values.

Falsifiable prediction. If stages are balanced and microbatches remain compute-bound, measured step time should track (P-1)/(m+P-1) within a few percent as m is swept. Systematic deviation indicates stage imbalance or microbatch underutilization, and the fix differs in each case.

Rollback gate. Adopt a new PP degree or schedule only if tokens/s/GPU improves and per-stage peak memory stays under the OOM headroom you had before, with a full checkpoint save/load verified under the new topology; otherwise revert.

source_user: Define pipeline parallelism and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Definition. Pipeline parallelism (PP) partitions a model by depth: contiguous groups of transformer layers are assigned to different devices (stages), and activations flow stage to stage as point-to-point sends/receives. It is distinct from tensor parallelism, which splits work inside a layer and requires all-reduce collectives; PP moves one activation tensor per stage boundary and needs no collective at all.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure. PP is the parallelism that makes a model fit at all when weights plus optimizer state exceed one device's memory and the interconnect is too weak for wide TP. Because the only cross-device traffic is a single activation tensor of size microbatch x seq x hidden x dtype_bytes per boundary, PP tolerates slow links (PCIe, Ethernet, cross-node) where TP would collapse. This is exactly why real multi-node deployments use TP inside a node (over NVLink) and PP across nodes (over IB/RoCE).

Concrete mechanism: microbatching against the pipeline bubble. With P stages and a single batch, P-1 stages idle at any moment. Splitting the global batch into m microbatches and using a 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) schedule overlaps them, giving bubble fraction approximately (P-1)/(m+P-1). With P=4 and m=1 the bubble is 75%; with m=16 it falls to about 16%; with m=64 to about 4.5%. 1F1B is preferred over naive GPipe scheduling because it caps in-flight activation memory at roughly P microbatches rather than m, at the same bubble fraction. Interleaved (virtual-stage) schedules cut the bubble further by giving each device several non-contiguous layer chunks, at the cost of more stage-boundary transfers.

Boundary condition. The bubble formula only holds while stages are balanced and microbatches are large enough to keep each GPU compute-bound. Two failure regions: (a) if per-stage compute times differ, throughput is set by the slowest stage and adding microbatches does not help - embedding and LM-head stages are the usual offenders and often need explicit layer rebalancing; (b) shrinking the microbatch to raise m eventually pushes each GEMM below the size where the GPU saturates, so per-microbatch time stops falling linearly and total step time rises even though the computed bubble fraction improves. There is therefore an optimum m, and it must be measured, not assumed. A third boundary applies specifically to inference: for autoregressive decode, one token depends on the previous one, so there are few independent microbatches to overlap and PP mostly adds latency; PP helps inference throughput mainly for prefill-heavy or high-concurrency serving, not for single-stream latency.

Evidence to collect before claiming PP is working: per-stage forward/backward wall time (to prove balance), measured bubble from a timeline trace rather than the formula, activation memory high-water mark per stage, stage-boundary transfer size and observed link bandwidth, and step time vs m swept over at least four values.

Falsifiable prediction. If stages are balanced and microbatches remain compute-bound, measured step time should track (P-1)/(m+P-1) within a few percent as m is swept. Systematic deviation indicates stage imbalance or microbatch underutilization, and the fix differs in each case.

Rollback gate. Adopt a new PP degree or schedule only if tokens/s/GPU improves and per-stage peak memory stays under the OOM headroom you had before, with a full checkpoint save/load verified under the new topology; otherwise revert.

source_user: Contrast pipeline parallelism with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer:
Contrast: pipeline parallelism (PP) versus the naive alternative of not using it.

The naive implementation. The model is placed on one device (or replicated whole across devices for data parallelism). If it fits, this is genuinely better: zero cross-device activation traffic, no bubble, no stage-balance problem, and the simplest failure and checkpointing story. Naive placement is the correct default and should only be abandoned when it demonstrably fails. Its failure mode is binary: once weights + gradients + optimizer state + activations exceed device memory, the job does not run slowly, it OOMs. The second naive option - offloading layers to host memory to force a fit - does run, but every offloaded layer pays a PCIe round trip per step, and step time typically degrades by an order of magnitude, which is far worse than the pipeline bubble PP would have cost.

What PP changes, mechanically. PP splits the layer stack into P contiguous stages, one per device, and passes only the boundary activation tensor (microbatch x seq x hidden x dtype_bytes) between stages as a point-to-point send/recv - no collectives. Memory per device drops roughly P-fold for weights and optimizer state, which is the entire point. The cost it introduces is the pipeline bubble: with a single batch, P-1 devices idle. Microbatching with a 1F1B schedule reduces the bubble fraction to approximately (P-1)/(m+P-1) for m microbatches; at P=4, m=16 that is about 16% idle. So the honest comparison is: naive placement is 0% bubble but infeasible; PP is feasible at a measurable, bounded efficiency loss; offload is feasible but usually far more expensive than that bounded loss.

Boundary condition. PP wins over the naive path only while (a) stages are balanced - throughput is set by the slowest stage, so an unbalanced split can be worse than offload; (b) microbatches stay large enough for each GEMM to saturate the GPU, otherwise raising m improves the bubble formula while worsening real step time; and (c) the workload has independent microbatches to overlap. Condition (c) is where the contrast inverts for inference: autoregressive decode is sequentially dependent, so PP adds per-token latency without a compensating overlap, and a naive single-device or TP-only placement is usually better for single-stream serving. PP is a training and prefill-heavy-serving technique, not a decode-latency technique.

Evidence required to justify choosing PP over the naive path: measured OOM point of the naive configuration with the real sequence length and batch (not an estimate), per-stage forward/backward times proving balance, timeline-derived bubble rather than the formula, step time swept over at least four values of m, activation high-water mark per stage, and stage-boundary transfer size against measured link bandwidth.

Falsifiable prediction. If PP is correctly balanced, end-to-end tokens/s should reach at least (1 - (P-1)/(m+P-1)) of the ideal linear scaling from the naive single-device rate. Falling materially short of that bound means imbalance or undersized microbatches - not an inherent PP cost - and should be diagnosed before accepting the configuration.

Rollback gate. Keep PP only if tokens/s/GPU beats every feasible alternative (offload, TP, ZeRO-3 sharding) on the same hardware and the same data, and a checkpoint save/restore round trip has been verified under the PP topology. Any failed criterion means revert to the previous configuration in the same window.
